author: rnegron
body:
## Problem

- On Depot-routed PRs, the `Report Depot migration results` check lands on another PR's head commit.
- The report ran on `pull_request_target`, whose runs share the base commit, and Depot attaches their checks by it: 35 of 42 sampled checks sat on the wrong PR.
- A failed report therefore shows red on an unrelated PR, and the owning PR shows no report check.
- The report itself (CI report sections, `Migration risk` check) reached the right PR.

## Changes

- Depot `check-migrations` now posts the Django SQL section, the risk section, the ClickHouse SQL section and the `Migration risk` check itself, as GitHub's job does.
- The sections post with a posthog-tests token limited to pull request writes, and each write skips when the mint fails, so the ambient Depot token never writes.
- The `Migration risk` check uses a second token with `checks:write` only, minted after the steps that run PR code, as in canonical.
- The `pull_request_target` workflow, its artifact handoff, the render script and the relay's `migrations` mode are gone.
- Mechanical: tests of the removed code go with it; the depot-ci skill reference records the misplaced-check measurement.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Depot check-migrations] --> B[(report artifacts)]
  C{{pull_request_target report}} -->|polls, downloads| B
  C --> D[CI report + Migration risk]
  C -.->|job check| E[another PR's head]
  classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
  classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
  classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
  class A,C phBlue; class B,D phGray; class E phRed;
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Depot check-migrations] --> D[CI report + Migration risk]
  classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
  classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
  class A phBlue; class D phGray;
```

## How did you test this code?

- Validated on [depot migration reports throwaway](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/106891) at `acaca69`, a Depot-routed copy of this branch plus one empty migration:
  - GitHub [handed the tests off](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36162372152/job/108161874439), and Depot [Validate migrations](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/runs/108162183245) passed.

- Until this merges, master's old report workflow still runs on this branch and its throwaway, and fails on the new artifact shape.
- Ran locally: the relay tests, `hogli test:workflows`, `hogli lint:workflows`, the Depot drift check, and actionlint on the Depot file (no new findings against master).

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, claude-opus-5-5

- Skills: `/depot-ci`, `/authoring-ci-workflows`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/writing-tests`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.

- `/code-review high`: fixed the `checks:write` token reaching PR code, the triplicated reporter guard, Node setup able to fail the job, and em dashes in comments. Other findings match canonical behavior, so they stay for a both-engine follow-up.

author: themiddnight
body:
## What this changes

This implements DEV-381, so someone outside the project can add content, open a PR, and get a verdict from the repo itself.

- **CI:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile` and then `bun run verify` as one step. It runs on every PR and on every push to `main`. The Bun version comes from the new `packageManager` field.
- **Golden test fix:** CI would have been red without this. The DEV-420 WAV hash depends on the platform, so the recorded hash never matches on Linux x64, while the call log does. This is the variance named as risk R2 in the DEV-420 spec. `renderMixdownGolden.wav.sha256` now holds one `<sha256> <platform>` line per recorded platform. That commit changes nothing else. The GitHub runner produces the same hash as the recorded `linux-x64` line.
- **Test isolation:** found on the first CI run. `bun test` runs every file in one process, in filesystem order, so CI's file order differs from a local one. That order exposed three tests that leaked state into later files:
  - Five store tests left `window` defined. That made axe-core, which `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` loads, crash in every ESLint-API test that ran after them.
  - `mixdownSnapshot.test.ts` left a drum solo in the store.
  - `leadRecord.test.ts` relied on the step resolution another file had set.

  Each test now cleans up after itself or sets the state it needs. The suite passes in the local order, in reverse order and in three shuffled file orders. The rule is recorded as R356 in `testing.md`.
- **Licence:** the code is under Apache-2.0 (`LICENSE`, `NOTICE`). `TRADEMARKS.md` reserves the Solna and murva names and the images under `public/assets/`. A fork may say it is "based on Solna", but a published fork must use its own name and icons.
- **Content checks:**
  - These are tests, not a new `check:presets` script. Most of the rules the card lists were already covered by tests.
  - `src/data/libraryEntries.test.ts` adds the missing generic rules for the three comp libraries.
  - `bun run check:content` runs just the content tests plus `check:drums` and `check:levels`, as a fast check for contributors. It stays out of `verify`, because `bun test` there already runs these tests.
- **Docs:**
  - `README.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`. CONTRIBUTING covers each content type, the `src/data/` literals-only rules, which tests fail and why, and the listening review.
  - A PR template that asks what a content addition sounds like and what it is for.
  - ADR-0053 with rules R351–R356.
  - CLAUDE.md now points to CONTRIBUTING instead of repeating it.

## Content additions

None.

## Checklist

- [x] `bun run verify` passes locally on Linux x64, and in CI
- [x] `bun run eslint` prints zero warnings
- [x] Content only: n/a

## Differences from the card

- The card asked for a `check:presets` script inside `verify`. This PR puts the rules in tests instead, so the same rules are not checked twice.
- The card says a drum grid has "seven rows × 16 steps". That no longer matches the code: rows are optional, there are eleven voices, and 3/4 and 6/8 grids are 12 steps.

author: maximefd
ahaarrestad
body:
Fixes two items from #4701's "Not fixed here": token revocation, and the refresh half of the empty-token case.

**A token the server rejects is never refreshed.** A refresh only happens once the stored expiry is within a minute, so a token revoked early 401s on every run until then. Now a 401 makes the next run refresh. Only 401 counts (RFC 6750); 403, 5xx and network errors are left alone, and nothing is armed without a stored refresh token and client id. A refresh that fails transiently is retried each run until it succeeds.

**A refresh without `access_token` wiped the stored token**, so the next upload went out as `Bearer `. That response now counts as a failed refresh and the old token is kept. If it also rotated the refresh token, the new one is dropped; the next refresh may then get `invalid_grant`, which asks the user to reconnect.

**Unchanged:** the constructor's `== null` guard, and the device-flow path (`pollForToken`). **Still open:** basal-injection deletes need nocturne-java 0.2.6+ and prefix matching; separate PR.

All green: `./gradlew :app:testFastDebugUnitTest :wear:testFastDebugUnitTest`

author: njoyimpeguy
body:
> **This PR must target `dev`, not `main`.** `main` holds what shipped and is
> the branch a tag is cut from; every change lands on `dev` first through a
> reviewed PR. Only release and hotfix branches open against `main`, and any
> other PR opened there is asked to retarget `dev` before review.

## Who made this change? (required)

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Written by | agent (controller), with agent implementers and independent reviewers |
| Model + exact id | Controller: `muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free` (Muse Spark 1.3 Free, opencode). Implementer and reviewers: `space-bunny-free`. |
| Harness + version | opencode |
| Installed plugins | augments-labs/sdlc-skills 10.3.0 (plan skills); no editor or language plugins used |
| Human who reviewed this diff | NjoyimPeguy |

## What problem did you hit?

The release check was a detached thread with no owner, and a cache file
under the user's home that the startup path read through a plain
`File::open`. Four defects, each observed before it was fixed:

- **It asked GitHub before the first frame was drawn.** The prose in three
  places, and the commit body, said "post-frame"; the code armed the
  request at `src/cli.rs` and the opening was not committed until
  `converse.rs` reached `opening.commit`. A default run with a stale cache
  could open a socket on the path the first frame is measured on.
- **The new uncredentialed GET was a credential sink.** It took a
  `&[(&str, &str)]` and copied each into the request. Any in-process caller
  could put an `Authorization` or API-key value on the wire to a
  caller-chosen URL with no redaction registered, while the doc said the
  route carried no credential. The first fix removed the header *list* but
  left a prepared `Outgoing` route that `set_header` fills and only
  `protect` registers — a convention, not a typed boundary. The landed
  route takes no caller header at all.
- **A hostile response could break the cache's one-line contract.** The tag
  was trimmed *before* the newline check, so `"\n1.2.3\n"` and `"1.2.3\r"`
  were accepted, and a tag of `"v"` became an empty name that was then
  written as an empty line. Both were reproduced before the fix.
- **A FIFO at the cache's name blocked the read before it was bounded.**
  `crucible_privacy::open_read` opened on Unix without `O_NONBLOCK`, so
  opening for reading waited on a writer. On the startup path that hangs
  the first frame with no bound; the fallback read after a failed request
  runs synchronously on a runtime worker, outside the request's own
  timeout, where `abort()` cannot interrupt a syscall.

## What does this PR change?

Adds `crucible-update`, which owns release discovery and the cached check as
work the application runtime owns, armed once per run behind the opening
being drawn. The GET route carries its two non-secret headers as private
constants, so no in-process caller can put a credential on it. A tag is
accepted only if it is one line, fits the cache line, and still has a name
after its single leading `v`. The protected read opens without waiting, and
`tighten` — the other pre-frame open in the same path — does too.

## What alternatives did you consider?

- **A typed wrapper around a caller-supplied header** was rejected: it
  still relies on the caller remembering `protect`, and a convention is
  what caused the finding. A route with no caller header cannot be
  misused.
- **Widening the blocking-thread pool further** was considered and is not
  done here. The cache write is a counted owner; with the foreground stops
  that #745 added, the pool is 16 against a counted 15, so one thread
  stays in spare. Both widenings were the accountable owner's decision,
  and the compile-time `assert!` is what holds them to it.
- **Bounding the lifecycle future at the caller** was rejected: the
  one-poll ledgered crossing is the spelling the repository's own
  invariants leave, and both in-tree backends answer in one poll.

## Is this one change?

Yes: the release check is owned work, and the ordering, the credential
route, the tag boundary and the blocking read are each a property of that
ownership rather than separable features.

## Which surfaces does it touch?

- **Security boundaries:** an outgoing network request and a file under the
  user's home. The request route carries no caller-chosen header; the
  protected read refuses links and non-regular files and does not wait for
  a writer. Independent security audits cleared the landed candidate on a
  fresh review of all four findings.
- **Durable formats:** the release cache is unchanged — same file name,
  same single-line shape, same 24 h freshness. It is read and written
  through the privacy owner, and the write is exclusive-create plus
  `sync_all` plus an atomic replace.
- **Generated files:** none.
- **Platform-specific behaviour:** the privacy read open is non-blocking on
  Unix; the Windows open refuses a reparse point by name and makes no such
  open. Both were verified against the source on a Linux host and are
  covered by the Windows cells.
- **Terminal rendering:** none.
- **Performance-sensitive paths:** startup, and the blocking-thread budget.
  The check is armed after the first frame and reads a bounded cache line;
  see Proof for the budget. The blocking pool is 16 against a counted 15
  after taking #745 in — that merge is why the figure is not 14.
- **Required-case obligations:** none rewritten.

## Prior PRs and issues

- [x] I searched open **and** closed PRs and issues for this problem or area.
- Related: #745 and #743 (merged immediately before this, and touching
  files this change also touches — the merge is taken in and was clean).
  #744 fixed a sandbox test whose failure message was truncated, the same
  "a diagnostic that lies" class this PR closes twice in `tagged`.

## Proof

`scripts/sh/check.sh` on the exact tree, after taking `dev` in:

```
GATE_EXIT:0
all deterministic gates passed
```

Which test failed before this change, and what it said:

- **Ordering.** `logs/round1/s01-ordering-red.log` — with the arm before
  the commit, the report read "with none of it drawn". The passing form
  requires the arm to happen after `opening.commit` succeeds.
- **Credential route.** a `compile_fail` doctest: against the base it
  "compiled successfully, but it's marked `compile_fail`"; after, the
  forbidden call is `E0599` (no method). Falsified by reintroducing the
  route.
- **Tag boundary.** the controller reproduced both directly — `"\n1.2.3\n"`
  was accepted as `1.2.3` and `"v"` produced an empty name. The four
  oracles fail against the old body and pass after.
- **FIFO.** the oracle's RED is a hang to its own bound; the falsification
  with the flag removed hangs again, restored by hash with
  `sha256sum -c` OK. It plants a real no-writer pipe, not a directory,
  which opens without waiting and would have witnessed nothing.
- **Blocking write placement.** a single-worker runtime catches it
  (`Some(ThreadId(3))`).
- **Blocking budget.** a compile-time falsification, one per direction,
  each restored byte-exact. The merge with #745 is a third: both units edited
  the same assert, the resolution counts both owners, and `cargo check
  -p crucible-app` compiled it clean — the `assert!` is the oracle, not the
  controller's arithmetic.
- **A test this change added, which flaked on CI.** `client::tests::
  idle_connections_are_reaped_by_the_pool_timer` failed on the macOS Intel
  cell with `Stalled(Answer)` and passed on a re-run. It is not a
  pre-existing flake: it does not exist at the base commit, and this change
  added both the 15-second pool idle timeout and the test for it. The
  mechanism is that `tokio` advances a *paused* clock to the next deadline
  whenever the runtime parks (`runtime/time/mod.rs:259`, after a zero-duration
  I/O poll when the time driver was not what woke it), so any park taken
  while the request's own one-minute answer bound is armed jumps the clock
  up to a minute

author: sergioazoc
body:
## Why

Tailwind generates CSS only for class names **written out in full**. A class put together at runtime gets none, and the element silently goes unstyled:
- `` `bg-${color}-500` ``
- `` `w-[${width}px]` ``
- `` `hover:${cls}` ``

In development it only works when the same class happens to be written out somewhere else.

## The rule

- **What it checks.** In the raw extractor view it looks at the token glued in front of each `${}`. It reports when that token starts with a Tailwind utility root or variant: `bg-`, `grid-cols-`, `-mt-`, `w-[`, `hover:`, `data-`.
- **How often.** Each runtime class is reported **once**. The class is read back from the source up to the first whitespace outside `${…}`, so the message quotes it as written, including `` `bg-${active ? 'blue' : 'gray'}-500` `` and `` `from-${a}-${b}` ``.
- **Not reported:** `` `${base} p-4` `` (a whole class comes from the variable), `` `icon-${name}` `` and `` `${a}-${b}` `` (the text isn't Tailwind's).
- **No autofix.**
- **DS-optional.**
  - With an entry point, the project's own utilities and variants count as roots, such as a `@theme` namespace like `bar-*`.
  - Without one it uses `STATIC_UTILITY_ROOTS` (150) and `STATIC_VARIANTS` (71). A test pins both lists to Tailwind's own class and variant lists, so they can't drift.
- **Documented limits, each with a test:**
  - `"bg-" + color` concatenation;
  - a variant chosen after the static text (`` `${bp}:flex` ``).

## Evidence

- **shadcn/ui apps/v4: 0 reports**, so no false positives on a large real codebase.
- `bench/synthetic/08-dynamic.tsx`: exactly the one expected report (`bg-${color}-500`).
- 28 rule tests, plus the static-list sync test and `fatal-errors`.

## Registration

The rule count goes from 24 to 25 everywhere, and docs-sync checks every count:
- EN/ES rule page;
- the rules index (Correctness list and the DS-optional table);
- both READMEs, with a section and the setup snippet;
- the setup **starter set**, as `error`;
- CLAUDE.md and the CHANGELOG.

Closes #763

## Summary

Adds a press and hold to open the large card preview on the practice table. A press on a card starts a 500 ms timer; when it fires, the preview fades in (100 ms) and the device vibrates where `navigator.vibrate` exists. The release hides the preview. The tap still opens the preview as before.

- `useCardHold` (`src/app/decks/practice/useCardHold.ts`): the timer, the 8 px cancel threshold (shared with the `PointerSensor`'s `activationConstraint`), the haptic pulse, and the `window`/`document` listeners that end a hold (`pointerup`, `pointercancel`, a second `pointerdown`, `blur`, `visibilitychange`). Its `onPointerDown` calls dnd-kit's own `onPointerDown`, so the drag keeps working. It swallows the click that follows a hold, and blocks the context menu.
- `page.tsx`: a separate `heldCardId` state is shown in place of `focusedCardId` while a hold is down, so the release puts back a tap-opened preview (owner answer 2) and never touches the crew panel. `handleDragStart` clears the hold.

Each `agent-browser` call takes hundreds of ms. Holding the crew card switched the preview to Naomi Wildman. The release brought back the ship's tap preview, and the crew panel stayed open (owner answer 2). |

| 3 | A press and release under 500 ms shows no preview | ✅ Pass. I sent `pointerdown` on the mission card, `pointerup` 250 ms later, and no `click`. There was no preview at 250 ms or at 1050 ms. In the same `eval`, a 650 ms press as a control did show the preview, and the release hid it. |

author: chrispader
body:
The benchmark's ordinary query loops do not show what happens when an app reuses a prepared statement or sends a native batch. This adds matched full-row and indexed point reads, explicit transaction inserts, and batch inserts where the library supports them. Every case checks its result, and the timed section includes binding and execution while setup and statement disposal stay outside it.

This draft depends on #1 for current library versions and #2 for repeatable runs and recorded SQLite settings. Because both branches are still open, this branch includes their commits and targets upstream `main`; its new work is in the `feat: benchmark prepared and batch SQLite APIs` commit. The ordinary and prepared pairs use identical SQL and parameters. The explicit transactions have separate labels from the callback transaction case, and expo-sqlite's missing native parameter batch API appears as unsupported. The normalized run also omits Expo's callback transaction because it opens a separate connection whose settings cannot be established outside the timer.

## Reproduction

Build the app in Release mode on iOS and Android. Open the benchmark, run both library defaults and normalized WAL/FULL modes, and check the per-case samples and shared manifest. Each run uses one warmup and three measured rounds by default; the JSON export includes samples, failures, checksums, PRAGMAs, and engine metadata. Compare matching query shapes and dispatch modes within one settings mode.

The combined dependency and benchmark changes passed Release builds and a bounded correctness run on a physical iPhone 13 Pro with iOS 26.5.2 and a Samsung SM-G977B with Android 12. Each mode used 50 rows and read repetitions, one warmup, three measured rounds, and a 50 ms cooldown. Across both devices, 618 measured samples completed without correctness failures. Normalized mode recorded the expected Expo callback-transaction omission. This checks the combined series, not isolated PR performance or the default 250-row run policy.

author: batmac
body:
`pre-commit.ci - pr` is currently red on every PR, including the latest merged one (#1188):

```
Validate JSON Schema files...............................................Failed
- hook id: check-metaschema
  .github/renovate.json::$.description: [...] is not of type 'string'
```

## Why
`check-metaschema` (check-jsonschema) runs on every JSON/YAML file (`types_or: [json, yaml]`) and validates each one **as a JSON Schema document**. JSON Schema requires `description` to be a string. Renovate accepts an array, and #1174 made the top-level `description` of `.github/renovate.json` an array.

The repo has no JSON Schema files: no tracked JSON/YAML file references `json-schema.org`. So on this repo the hook can only produce false positives. This PR removes it.

If you'd rather keep it for future schema files, the alternative is `exclude: ^\.github/renovate\.json$` on the hook.

## Testing
- Reproduced before the change: `check-jsonschema --check-metaschema .github/renovate.json` exits 1 with the error above.
- After the change: `SKIP=golangci-lint,renovate-config-validator pre-commit run --all-files` (the same skips as pre-commit.ci) passes every hook.

author: djay
body:
The admin test helpers wait for the thing they're waiting for, never a guessed number of milliseconds. There were 39 fixed waits in `AdminUIHelper`; the only ones left pace demo recordings, and run only while a clip is being recorded.

## Why
A fixed wait is either too short, so the check runs before the thing happened, or too long, which slows the suite and can swallow an author's action. The one that surfaced it: `navigateToParentBlock` re-checked the selection 300ms after stepping up. On a slow page it read the old selection, took that as "not there yet", and stepped up again, past the target. It went from a tab onto its tabs block, so + opened the block chooser instead of adding a tab.

## What each helper now waits on
| Helper | Waits for |
|---|---|
| `navigateToParentBlock` | the sidebar to lose a level |
| `escapeToParent` | the sidebar to lose a level, or the bridge's edit mode to go text → block, whichever happened (then Escape again) |
| `copyAndGetClipboardText`, `cutSelectedText` | the clipboard to change from a marker set first |
| `pasteFromClipboard`, `getBlockTextInIframe` | nothing extra; the caller asserts the result with a retrying expect |
| `selectTextRange`, `selectTextAcrossBlocks` | the `selectionchange` they cause (the bridge's listener, added earlier, has handled it by then) |
| `waitForStableSelection` | the expected selection while the bridge is idle (no render, transform or block), not "unchanged for 200ms", which can't tell settled from not started |
| `longPressBlock` | the bridge's own long-press timer to fire |
| drag moves, auto-scroll steps, UI-position polling | one drawn frame (`nextFrame`) |
| `completeDrag` | the drag shadow to be gone |
| `moveToSafeZone` | the iframe's scroll position to stay the same from one frame to the next |
| `openSidebarTab`, `dragDropImageFile` | the element to be in view |
| fieldset accordions, chooser sections | their `active` class |
| `typeInlineText` (replace) | the field's text to be selected |
| `waitForBlockCountToBe`, `waitForFieldValueToBe`, `waitForLinkEditorPopup` | `expect.poll` in place of hand-written loops with sleeps |

## Checked locally (admin-mock)
- `inline-editing-clipboard` and `inline-editing-links`: 17/17.
- `drag-and-drop` plus the parent-navigation and Escape tests in `container-blocks`: 41/41.
- Type errors in the helper are unchanged from main.

author: octalide
body:
Closes #900

## What changed

- `raw_move` and `raw_copy` share two private kernels, `copy_forward` and `copy_backward`. `raw_copy` runs forward. `raw_move` runs backward only when dst lies inside the source range (`d - s < n`, unsigned), and forward otherwise.
- **x86_64 and aarch64:** 16-byte unaligned vectors (`movups`, `ldr/str q`, checked in the disassembly). A copy of up to 32 bytes loads its first and last chunk (16/8/4/2/1 bytes) before storing either, so it is overlap-safe in both directions. A longer copy loads both 16-byte ends first, then walks a body aligned to dst in 64-byte steps with every load of a step before its stores, then stores the ends. So unaligned heads and tails cost two overlapping stores rather than a byte loop.
- **riscv64 and anything else:** machine words when src and dst are co-aligned, bytes otherwise. `u8x16` scalarizes to 16 byte moves there (checked in the disassembly), and a misaligned word may trap or be emulated.
- The results are byte-for-byte what they were. `memory.move` goes through `raw_move` and gets faster with it.

## Decisions the issue left open

- **No `rep movsb`.** It was measured on this host (Ryzen 7 5800X3D, `erms` and `fsrm` in cpuinfo) against the vector loop, in the same exploratory run (before `agent-heavy --exclusive` was used for the final numbers, so these are indicative). With dst misaligned by 3 it took 334 µs per 1 MiB and 368 ns per 1 KiB, against 31 µs and 26 ns for the 64-byte vector loop. With a forward overlap it took 71 to 77 µs per 1 MiB against 26 to 27 µs. It only tied or lost when co-aligned (34 µs against 28 µs). Backward `rep movsb` is slow everywhere. There is also no `erms` name in the compiler's extension vocabulary or in `std.system.cpu.Features`, so a gate would need a separate cpuid probe for no gain.
- **64-byte steps over 16-byte ones.** In the same run the 16-byte loop took 41 µs per 1 MiB backward against 25 to 27 µs with 64-byte steps, and 46 ns per 1 KiB backward against 25 ns.
- **`copy[T]` is left as it is.** It copies element by element, which is word-wide or wider for most T. Routing it through `raw_copy` would add a `*T` to `ptr` cast for every T, including secret-qualified ones. The issue does not ask for it.

## Secrecy

`raw_move`, `raw_copy` and `move[T]` take `ptr`, and their branches depend only on addresses and lengths, as before. No `#[oblivious]` function calls them. An awk scan found 363 `#[oblivious]` functions across std, crypto, tls, quic, http, acme, hedge and laurel, and none of them calls these. The sanity check on the scan was that it found `copy_secret`. Secret storage uses `memory.secret.copy_secret`, which this PR does not touch. The only `memory.move[T]` caller that handles key material (`mach-crypto` `encode_public_der`) moves a public key.

## Benchmarks: 1 KiB and 1 MiB

Setup: the same bench source built against std v8.0.0 (before, binary sha256 `803ba20ebcbfc410`) and against this branch's `memory.mach` (after, `a785eb157a576f63`). Release profile, mach 5.12.0 (the official tarball, checked against SHA256SUMS), x86_64-linux, Ryzen 7 5800X3D. It ran under `agent-heavy --exclusive` from 14:43:23 to 14:43:45. The 1-minute load average was 2.60 to 3.12, from non-heavy processes outside the lock. In `vmstat 1` alongside, swap-out was 0 and swap-in peaked at 1020 KB/s in one second. Each figure is the median ns per call over 9 batches. It is the median of three runs, and the three agreed within 3% except where noted.

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| raw_move 1 KiB, forward overlap (dst 64 below) | 312.6 ns | 24.2 ns |
| raw_move 1 KiB, backward overlap (dst 64 above) | 312.6 ns | 24.8 ns |
| raw_move 1 KiB, disjoint, co-aligned / misaligned | 23.3 / 23.9 ns | 23.9 / 24.2 ns |
| raw_copy 1 KiB, disjoint, co-aligned / misaligned | 86.5 / 25.4 ns | 23.3 / 23.6 ns |
| raw_move 1 MiB, forward overlap (dst 16 KiB+3 below) | 311.9 µs | 29.2 µs |
| raw_move 1 MiB, forward overlap (dst 1 KiB+5 below) | 311.8 µs | 28.2 µs |
| raw_move 1 MiB, backward overlap (dst 16 KiB+3 above) | 316.2 µs | 28.5 µs |
| raw_move 1 MiB, disjoint, co-aligned / misaligned | 27.6 / 35.8 µs | 25.3 / 30.7 µs |
| raw_copy 1 MiB, disjoint, co-aligned / misaligned | 81.5 / 34.1 µs | 25.3 / 30.5 µs |

Disjoint `raw_move` was already fast before, because the release pipeline's vectorizer rewrites its byte loop when the ranges cannot alias. An overlapping move, which is what hedge's compaction does, stayed byte-wise. That case is now 11x to 13x faster. The co-aligned `raw_copy` word loop was slower than the vectorized byte loop, and it is now 3.2x to 3.7x faster. The before disjoint-misaligned figures varied by up to 15% across runs, and the after figures by under 1%.

## hedge's lane: cache shard lock hold times (hedge#285 workload)

Setup: a scratch clone of hedge `origin/dev` (0c4c69b, which pins std v8.0.0), with temporary instrumentation that is not committed anywhere. It records lock-to-unlock time per shard, tagged by operation, in `store.release`, in log2 ns buckets. The workload reproduces hedge#290's measurement: 8 threads, 8 shards, an 8 MiB arena, 128 slots, 64 keys, memory bodies of 1 KiB to 256 KiB (plus 0 to 60 odd bytes, so compaction runs at arbitrary alignment) and 1 MiB disk bodies, read and written in 16 KiB chunks, 3000 operations per thread (70% read, 20% record, 10% invalidate). Every read verifies its body byte for byte, and all 10 runs had 0 failures. The before binary is std v8.0.0 (sha256 `1ae678e6fa0fa42f`), and the after binary is std v8.0.0 with only `src/memory.mach` replaced by this branch's (`e93ce92cb57d684f`). Both are release builds. They ran alternately, 5 runs each, in the same `agent-heavy --exclusive` window as the table above. The p99 is a log2 bucket upper bound. Max is the range across the 5 runs.

| operation | before mean | before p99 ≤ | before max | after mean | after p99 ≤ | after max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| begin (includes eviction) | 13.5–15.7 µs | 262–524 µs | 0.70–0.89 ms | 2.5–2.7 µs | 33 µs | 48–111 µs |
| commit (includes supersede) | 18.1–21.2 µs | 262 µs | 0.31–0.57 ms | 2.8–2.9 µs | 33 µs | 26–87 µs |
| invalidate | 13.3–14.6 µs | 262 µs | 0.23–0.35 ms | 2.1–2.3 µs | 16–33 µs | 29–103 µs |
| unpin | 0.67–0.73 µs | 1 µs | 0.16–0.32 ms | 0.53–0.54 µs | 1 µs | 19–52 µs |
| memory read, 16 KiB | 1.16–1.30 µs | 4 µs | 0.25–0.33 ms | 0.89–0.91 µs | 2 µs | 0.22–0.27 ms |
| memory write, 16 KiB | 1.05–1.19 µs | 4 µs | 0.34–0.38 ms | 0.99–1.03 µs | 2 µs | 0.24–0.38 ms |
| select + pin | 0.61–0.67 µs | 1–2 µs | 7–52 µs | 0.60–0.62 µs | 1 µs | 7–48 µs |
| disk read setup | 0.54–0.58 µs | 1 µs | 48–97 µs | 0.55 µs | 1 µs | 45–51 µs |

The compaction tail is gone. The operations that compact (begin, commit, invalidate, and unpin through a deferred reclaim) went from a 0.2 to 0.9 ms maximum to about 0.1 ms or less. The remaining 0.2 to 0.4 ms maxima on 16 KiB reads and writes are unchanged, before and after. They are not moves, since a 16 KiB copy takes about 0.5 µs. Most likely they are preemption with 8 threads on this host.

## Tests

- `std.memory.raw_move:byte_exact_sweep` and `std.memory.raw_copy:byte_exact_sweep` check against a reference that stages the source first. They cover every length 0 to 64, a 37-byte stride to 4 KiB, and each power of two from 128 to 4096 with its neighbours. They cover every source phase of a 16-byte chunk up to 64 bytes and 4 phases above that. They cover dst below and above src, both disjoint (touching and 33 bytes apart) and overlapping by 1, 7, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17, 31, 32, 33, 63, 64, 65, 100, 127, 128, 129 and 1000 bytes, plus dst == src. The whole window from 32 bytes before to 32 bytes after both ranges must match, so a stray write fails the test.
- **Counterfactual:** with one backward vector store taken from the wrong chunk, and the portable backward word loop reading one byte off, both sweeps' `raw_move` case failed with exit 7 (backward overlap) on x86_64 and on riscv6

author: simlarsen
body:
## Why

Master fixed the `k8s-high-cpu` numerator in 32c64851ed and fa7fe89b85: the agent chart now enables `k8s.node.cpu.usage` and `k8s.pod.cpu.usage` in kubeletstats, and the template is pinned to `.usage`. Two gaps in the test net let the bug ship, though, and one of them still exists:

- The Kubernetes alert-template sweep checked only `k8s.*` and `container.*` names. It skipped the undotted Prometheus-scraped metrics.
- Nothing checked the Kubernetes **dashboard** templates against what the agent sends. That's how the dashboard's four CPU widgets shipped reading `k8s.{node,pod}.cpu.usage` before the chart enabled them.

## Changes

- **Alert templates:** `no template queries a metric the agent does not emit` now covers every query of every Kubernetes alert template, not only `k8s.*` and `container.*` names.
- **Dashboard templates:** the new `Tests/Types/Dashboard/KubernetesDashboardTemplates.test.ts` requires every widget metric in the Kubernetes and Kubernetes Cost dashboards to be in `AGENT_EMITTED_METRIC_NAMES`. It collects every `filterData.metricName` in a widget's arguments, so a multi-query widget can't hide one.
- **`AGENT_EMITTED_METRIC_NAMES`:** the set now includes the chart's allowlisted Prometheus scrapes (cAdvisor, kube-state-metrics and the cost engine), read directly from `values.yaml` so they can't drift.
  - Each job keeps exactly `^(allowlist)$`.
  - The v0.96.0 prometheus receiver trims `_total` and unit suffixes only under `trim_metric_suffixes`, which defaults to off and the chart never sets. So the names arrive verbatim.

## Verification

- **Ran:**
  - `Tests/Types/Dashboard/*`, `KubernetesAlertTemplates`, `KubernetesMetricCatalog` and `KubernetesTemplateGroupByKeys`: 402 passed.
  - ESLint on the changed files: clean.
- **Mutation check:** misspelling `scheduler_pending_pods` in its template, or `node_cpu_hourly_cost` in the cost dashboard, now fails the new sweeps. Master's `^(k8s|container)\.` filter skipped the first, and nothing covered the second.
- **`npm run compile` in `packages/Common` fails on master itself**, independent of this PR: `MonitorCriteriaEvaluator.ts` imports `MetricsViewConfig` twice (lines 77 and 135, from 298e1c8e06 and 3ccc860243). This PR changes only test files; `tsc` reports no errors in them.

## Not in this PR

The `references only catalog metrics` test still skips `k8s.node.cpu.usage` through `NOT_EMITTED_BY_THE_PINNED_AGENT`. That entry's comment is now stale, because the chart emits the metric. Removing the entry needs a catalog entry for `k8s.node.cpu.usage`, which would show up in the Kubernetes metric picker next to the existing `k8s.node.cpu.utilization` "Node CPU Usage" entry. That's a product choice, so it's left for a follow-up.

author: jayanez
body:
## Summary

Continue the priority M2 performance goal on a separate, stacked track over draft PR #139. The current prototype removes redundant private-tree integration work and polls short Git children every 1 ms. Candidate and equally optimized serial lanes use the same poll interval. The T003 runner rejects this changed prototype until a renewed exact-input founder decision exists. The reviewed T003 negative result and the source PR commits remain unchanged.

## Evidence

- [Method, phase breakdown, results and limits](https://github.com/jayanez/agent-braid/blob/7d1a07775c2663da93e369ceccf5a8b352c28e78/docs/experiments/M2_PARALLEL_PREPARATION.md), with raw [small-fixture data](https://github.com/jayanez/agent-braid/blob/7d1a07775c2663da93e369ceccf5a8b352c28e78/docs/experiments/evidence/m2-parallel-preparation-synthetic-30.json) and two independent [shape-proxy runs A](https://github.com/jayanez/agent-braid/blob/7d1a07775c2663da93e369ceccf5a8b352c28e78/docs/experiments/evidence/m2-parallel-preparation-shape-30-a.json) and [B](https://github.com/jayanez/agent-braid/blob/7d1a07775c2663da93e369ceccf5a8b352c28e78/docs/experiments/evidence/m2-parallel-preparation-shape-30-b.json).
- The synthetic two-workstream proxy matches the reviewed corpus's three/five changed-path counts and patch sizes within 5%. In two 30-pair runs, median gain versus serial was **11.11%** and **13.64%**; pooled paired median was **12.54%** (95% bootstrap interval **10.82% to 13.67%**). Pooled gain versus the timed path-overlap baseline was **36.82%** (interval **34.78% to 40.10%**). Candidate, serial and path-baseline trees matched in all samples, sources stayed unchanged and unsafe admissions were zero.
- The small three-operation fixture reached **9.997%** versus serial, below the 10% threshold. The proxy does not reproduce actual code, history or hunk layout. **The M2 goal remains open until a changed-code real-corpus result is authorized and verified.** Both schedulers formed the same single wave on disjoint paths; the path-baseline gain is implementation cost reduction, not a scheduling advantage.
- Focused controls, Spec Kit, and both local `quick` and `pr` validation profiles passed in the pinned offline Linux ARM64 image. Each profile ran **184 tests, two skipped**, plus contracts, scientific controls and publication checks.

## Review boundary

Please review the 1 ms process poll and its unchanged failure controls, first-operation fast path, paired measurement and proxy calibration, and the explicit T003 code-hash rejection. These are synthetic engineering measurements. A new ADR 0015 real-workload experiment needs a separate founder decision binding exact code, command, image, dependencies and observation protocol. This draft requests no merge, execution authorization, independent-validation claim or M2 closure.

body: https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mr-boxington/trails/57 The landing-page showreel added in #553 now plays from an MP4 instead of being drawn live on a canvas. The same video also plays in link previews that support video. ## On the landing page - A native video player shows the showreel at 1920×1080, with standard controls and sound. - It does not autoplay. Until someone presses play it shows a poster frame (the "projects, worktrees, and CI." lockup), and with `preload="none"` nothing downloads before then. - Screen readers get the same per-chapter text description as before, including the published benchmark numbers. - The canvas player, its Web Audio scheduling, and its custom controls are gone from the page. The reel's TypeScript stays in the repo because it is what renders the video. ## In link previews The homepage now carries the same MP4 as `og:video`: ```html ``` - iMessage downloads the MP4 and autoplays it muted (Apple TN3156). - Discord plays an `og:video` MP4 inline when `og:type` is `video.other`. - Telegram usually attaches it as a playable video. - X and most other networks keep showing the 1200×630 image; `twitter:card` stays `summary_large_image`. X's web client plays link-card video only from YouTube, SoundCloud, and Periscope embeds, and a player card from any other domain renders no card at all. To show the reel playing on X, upload the MP4 to the post. ## How the video is made `docs/.vitepress/showreel-video.mjs` renders the reel frame by frame in headless Chromium and renders the score offline, both for the reel's own duration. It encodes 1080p60 H.264 High (level 4.2) with AAC and the index at the front, and writes the poster JPEG. The current render is about 3.7 MB and 15.0 s long, at -16.5 LUFS. The reel's chapter label rolls in its title row at the top, so the bottom edge stays clear for the player's controls. Both files are written beside their targets and renamed into place only after ffmpeg succeeds. - The docs workflow caches the render with `actions/cache`, keyed on the renderer, the reel's sources, the font, `benchmarks/results.json`, and the docs lockfile. On a cache miss it installs ffmpeg and Playwright's Chromium headless shell and runs `mise run render:showreel` before building. The video therefore always matches the current reel and the latest benchmark numbers, neither file is committed, and the versioned URL only changes when an input does. Renders of the same inputs are not byte-identical, so without the cache the URL would change on every deploy. - A `showreel.data.ts` loader gives the page and the meta tags versioned URLs (`?v=` is a content hash), so browsers and previews that cached an older render fetch the new one. - Local builds without a render leave the showreel section and the video tags out. `mise run render:showreel` renders both files; it needs ffmpeg and `aube exec playwright-core install chromium-headless-shell`. - New docs dev dependencies: `playwright-core` and `esbuild` (pinned to the version Vite already uses). ## Docs CI - Both docs jobs move from Namespace to GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners. The mbx bootstrap that `check:docs` needs uses `Swatinem/rust-cache`, which the repo's other GitHub-runner jobs already use and which saves only from `main`. The build timeout goes from 15 to 20 minutes to cover a cold Rust build plus the render. - Pull requests that touch the docs now run the same build job, render included, as a dry run. Only `main` uploads and deploys. PRs read `main`'s caches, and whatever a PR saves stays scoped to that PR. - Because the build job now runs pull request code, its token is read-only (`contents: read`, `pages: read`). `pages: write` and `id-token: write` stay on the deploy job, which runs only on `main`. - `check-social-images.mjs` now requires the homepage's `og:video` tags when the video is present, with a version that matches the file, an MP4 file, and a JPEG poster. It also requires every other page, and every page of a build without the video, to be `og:type=website` with no video tags. ## Validation - `mise run render:showreel` takes 85 s on the dev box. `ffprobe` reports H.264 High 4.2 at 1920×1080 and 60 fps, AAC 48 kHz stereo, and 15.000 s, with `moov` ahead of `mdat`. - `aube run docs:build` and the offline `lychee` link check pass with and without a render. - The metadata check fails as intended on a stale `?v=`, and when the video is present but the homepage tags are missing. A failing ffmpeg left the existing video byte-identical, with no partial file behind. - I tested the built site in Chromium at 1440×900 and 390×844. The video is paused after load and after scrolling into view, and it makes no MP4 request before play. On play it runs at 1920×1080 with sound. There is no horizontal scroll and no console errors. - `zizmor` (v1.30.1, as in CI) reports no findings for the updated workflow. - This PR's docs run is the dry run of the new workflow on a GitHub runner. From a cold cache, with the render, it passed in 5 min 22 s. Not verified: the link preview behavior in Discord and iMessage comes from the platforms' documentation, not a live post. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Stack created with GitHub Stacks CLI • Give Feedback 💬 --- > [!NOTE] > **Low Risk** > Changes are limited to docs site, CI, and marketing assets; no runtime product or auth paths. CI complexity and longer builds are the main operational note. > > **Overview** > The landing-page showreel is **pre-rendered to MP4** (and a poster) instead of drawn live in the browser. A new **`showreel-video.mjs`** pipeline uses headless Chromium and **ffmpeg** to encode 1080p60 H.264 with the offline score; **`mise run render:showreel`** and CI run it before docs builds, with **Actions cache** keyed on reel sources, benchmarks, and lockfile so deploy URLs stay stable. > > **`HomeShowreel.vue`** shrinks to a native **`

body: Closes #8796. Follows the benchmark baseline in [#8797](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/8797). ## Why we make these changes Replaying text deltas currently materializes and recopies the growing text prefix for every event. Reuse the existing string buffer for exact `TextPart`/`TextPartDelta` instances. Apply metadata eagerly to preserve independent snapshots, and retain the original path for other parts, custom subclasses, and invalid event ordering. ## New public surface None. ## User-visible behavior ```diff pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/models/__init__.py :: CompletedStreamedResponse.__aiter__() └─ pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/models/__init__.py :: CompletedStreamedResponse._iter_buffered() └─ pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/_parts_manager.py :: ModelResponsePartsManager.apply_event() - └─ pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/messages.py :: TextPartDelta.apply() - rebuild the growing prefix + ├─ pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/_parts_manager.py :: ModelResponsePartsManager._apply_metadata_or_copy_provider_details() - retain fresh metadata snapshots + └─ pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/_parts_manager.py :: ModelResponsePartsManager._buffer_string_delta() - materialize text only when read ``` ## Verification - Keep the merged 1,000/5,000-chunk benchmarks unchanged; [the Graviton baseline on `main`](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/actions/runs/36172070970) uploaded successfully. - [Public replay tests](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/8799/files#diff-d960bb61fde148c9fabda1375f3cb82be40ccc75ac1260cb4353d26cfcedb5d1) cover intermediate reads, retained snapshots, metadata updates, sparse indexes, custom part constructors/custom delta methods, missing starts, and cancellation. - Ten new compatibility cases pass against both implementations. A mutation probe verifies that conditional cloning would leak metadata from retained start events. - Python 3.14: 283 targeted tests passed, three expected failures. The new paths and tests have 100% line/branch coverage; Pyright, Ruff, pre-commit, and CI checks passed. - [Three independent matched baseline/head Graviton comparisons](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/8799#issuecomment-5837648536) showed 1,000 chunks falling from 30.7-30.8 ms to 19.0-19.3 ms (about 37-38% less time), and 5,000 chunks from 609.8-695.9 ms to 92.4-93.7 ms (about 85-87% less time). The large baseline remains variable, but the optimized measurements stayed tightly grouped. ## What changes for existing users Completed text streams replay without repeated prefix copying. Live streaming, event objects/order, non-text replay, and custom part/delta behavior remain unchanged. ### Checklist - [ ] Any **AI generated code** has been reviewed line-by-line by the human PR author, who stands by it. - [x] No **breaking changes** in accordance with the [version policy](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/blob/main/docs/version-policy.md). - [ ] Any permitted **compatibility impact** has a label, warning, migration, release note, and exact API-check waiver. - [x] **PR title** is fit for the [release changelog](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/releases). ## AI Disclaimer This PR was developed with the assistance of either Claude or Codex. I've reviewed and verified the changes.

author: alajmah
usehoplite[bot]
body:
## Summary

A coding-agent harness in the style of the "jev + opus 5.5" post. The worker model (Claude Opus 5.5, or any model you plug in) does the reasoning. Jev, TypeSafe's typed decision API, makes the small decisions. Jev can only pick one of the options the host prepares, or abstain. The host checks the pick again before it acts and records the outcome.

![jev-harness running the demo task](https://github.com/AvixoSec/jev-harness/blob/14bc372c6ef1dee950075e71023582cfd80baee1/docs/screenshot.jpg?raw=true)

## What's included

- **Harness server** (`src/server`, Hono + SSE): the session loop and a decision engine covering notes, route, step, model, effort, check, recover and compact. It talks to hosted Jev (`POST /v1/systemone`) or an offline simulated backend. Workers can be Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible or a scripted demo worker. It also has sandboxed file and shell tools and finds project notes (`AGENTS.md`, `.jev/notes`) and checks (`.jev/checks.json` or detected scripts).
- **Custom providers**: under **Settings → Custom providers**, paste a base URL, a key and model ids for any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API. There are presets for OpenRouter, DeepSeek, OpenAI, Groq, Together, Mistral, xAI, Ollama, LM Studio and an Anthropic-compatible proxy. You can fetch the model list and test the connection. Enabled providers become route candidates alongside Opus 5.5. You can also set them with `CUSTOM_BASE_URL` / `CUSTOM_API_KEY` / `CUSTOM_MODELS`, and the Jev endpoint can be swapped too.
- **Web UI** (`src/web`, React + Vite), following the post's video. The left side shows metrics, a lane timeline and latency and context charts. The middle shows the transcript with live decision cards and approval prompts. The right side is the Jev panel: host options → Jev scores → typed result → host checks → record.
- **Demo workspace** (`examples/tokenizer`): a small tokenizer with a real escaped-quote bug, so the whole flow runs without keys.
- **Guardrails**:
  - Mutating API calls need a loopback `Host` and an `x-jev-harness` header.
  - Keys stay on the server in a 0600 config, and the UI only sees the last four characters.
  - Harness keys are removed from the environment of commands the worker runs.
  - The workspace refuses `..` and symlink escapes.
  - Shell commands and checks need your approval.

body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unhelpful retries during Skill Workshop learning when an agent mixes Workshop proposal arguments with personal-library operations.

## User Impact

Agents receive explicit target, action, identifier, and list-limit guidance, plus useful field-level errors for rejected personal-library calls. Existing default routing, strict validation, and publication permissions remain in place.

## Why This Change Was Made

A real Learn flow sent Workshop fields to the personal library. Even correcting a list limit to 50 still failed because personal lists do not accept `limit`. Provider normalization combines the two argument surfaces, and Codex can [remove property descriptions from large schemas](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/50d77959bf927293c4b5ddcca81d05331ae582ea/codex-rs/tools/src/json_schema/compaction.rs). The essential Workshop guidance now lives in the existing [preserved top-level description](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/50d77959bf927293c4b5ddcca81d05331ae582ea/codex-rs/tools/src/dynamic_tool.rs). Personal validation reports bounded field paths and expected constraints without echoing supplied values. The same observed flow also exposed a missing `sessions_search` limit description; it now states the existing maximum of 25.

## Evidence

- The real combined-tool factory and normalization regression fails against the original generic error and passes with the repair. It exercises both list destinations and rejects unsupported personal fields, invalid actions, oversized identifiers, and oversized nested content.
- Full existing suites passed: Workshop 19 cases, session search 18 cases, and unchanged personal-authority/worker coverage 7 cases. Final description and fixture refinements passed the two affected focused cases.
- Captured actual OpenClaw-to-Codex tool descriptors verify guidance placement. Native transformation behavior is supported by the pinned dependency source above; this is not a captured provider request or a new live-model run.
- Core production and owning tool-test types, targeted lint/format, line and assertion ratchets, import-cycle checks, and docs links passed. Fresh managed review found no actionable P0–P2 issues.

Test cost: `pnpm test src/agents/tools/skill-workshop-tool.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` took 69.082 seconds on the original file and 43.953 seconds with the candidate; both included about 21 seconds of worker preparation. Import/cache warmth and host load were not controlled, so this is not a speedup claim. The extended existing case took 622 ms. `pnpm test src/agents/tools/sessions-search-tool.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` took 9.454 seconds, and the unchanged personal-authority suite took 10.935 seconds. Hosted CI run 36174669004 exposed a missing generated prompt update: `check-prompt-snapshots` failed after 77 seconds (29.1 seconds in the generator), and fail-fast cancelled sibling work. The canonical generator now records only the session-search description and its derived counts/hashes; `pnpm prompt:snapshots:check` passes in 25.894 seconds. All snapshot checks remain enabled. Replacement run 36176117081 passed: 140 jobs succeeded and 19 scope-selected jobs skipped over 15 minutes 43 seconds; the corrected hosted snapshot job passed in 69 seconds. Per-file hosted test durations were not isolated.

An initial test extension reached a real database-broker requirement in the wrong fixture. It was removed, and the combined proof now shares the existing broker-admitted Workshop fixture. An initial test-only type error was corrected without casts. Both failed attempts are retained in local evidence.

author: ryancotterell
body:
## What

Adds `analysis/item_level_reanalysis.R`, a small companion to `analysis_surp.Rmd`
that runs the surprisal delta-log-likelihood test while respecting the MECO items
(the 12 texts, one per `trialid`), and prints a table comparing it to the released
per-word test.

## Why the per-word test is anti-conservative

The released significance test counts each word as an independent observation: it
runs a one-sample sign-flip permutation test over the ~2000 per-word held-out
delta log-likelihoods, and that permutation null assumes the words are mutually
independent. They are not:

- Reading times are averaged across participants per word, but the resulting
  per-word values still cluster by text: words in the same passage share topic,
  position, and difficulty, so their delta log-likelihoods are positively correlated.
- With ~2000 correlated words nested in only 12 texts, the variance of the mean
  delta log-likelihood under the per-word permutation null is far smaller than its
  true sampling variance. The permutation distribution is too narrow, so the
  p-values come out too small.

The effective number of independent units is the 12 texts, not the ~2000 words.
Counting words as independent replicates fabricates precision: the test behaves as
if it had far more independent data than it does. The mismatch is visible below,
where the variance-explained gain from surprisal (`dR2`) is small (about 0.5 to
1.6 percent on top of a 65 to 73 percent baseline) yet the per-word test reports
p about 0.001. The point estimate is unaffected; only the stated certainty is wrong.

## Three minimal changes

Same delta-log-likelihood contrast, but each addressing one part of the above:
1. an item random intercept `(1 | trialid)`, so between-text variance is modeled
   rather than ignored;
2. leave-one-text-out folds (no text split across train/test), with the held-out
   density using the mixed-model predictive spread `sqrt(sigma^2 + tau^2)`, so the
   held-out fit is not inflated by same-text leakage;
3. the sign-flip permutation runs over the per-text mean delta log-likelihoods
   (12 independent units), with Benjamini-Hochberg across the reported cells.

The script also reports held-out R^2 (leave-one-text-out): baseline, full model,
and the gain from surprisal (`dR2`). The released per-word test is computed
alongside; the sign-flip permutation is spelled out (equivalent to the one-sample
`jmuOutlier::perm.test`) so the script needs only `lme4`.

## Model labels

- `mgpt_sc` - multilingual GPT (mGPT), surprisal from sentence context only
- `mgpt_lc` - mGPT, surprisal from long context (the whole preceding passage)
- `monot_30m` - a monolingual transformer (monolingual GPT trained from scratch), 30M training words
- `monot_all` - the same monolingual transformer, trained on the full corpus

## Run

```
cd analysis
Rscript item_level_reanalysis.R --lang en
```

## Result (English)

### Effect size: delta log-likelihood and variance explained

`dLL` is the mean per-word held-out delta log-likelihood (surprisal over baseline);
`dR2` is the held-out variance-explained gain from surprisal; `r2_full` is the full
model's held-out R^2. The effect is real and positive in every cell, and small.

```
 model      measure            dLL      dR2   r2_full
 mgpt_sc    gaze_rt        0.01180   0.0065     0.726
 mgpt_sc    total_rt       0.01980   0.0128     0.683
 mgpt_sc    firstfix_rt    0.00963   0.0064     0.653
 mgpt_lc    gaze_rt        0.01756   0.0096     0.730
 mgpt_lc    total_rt       0.02533   0.0164     0.690
 mgpt_lc    firstfix_rt    0.01393   0.0097     0.659
 monot_30m  gaze_rt        0.01185   0.0066     0.727
 monot_30m  total_rt       0.01389   0.0092     0.682
 monot_30m  firstfix_rt    0.00659   0.0047     0.655
 monot_all  gaze_rt        0.01148   0.0065     0.727
 monot_all  total_rt       0.01405   0.0092     0.682
 monot_all  firstfix_rt    0.00772   0.0056     0.656
```

### Significance: released per-word vs item-level, with BH

`p_word` / `p_item` are the released per-word test and the item-level test; the
`_BH` columns are Benjamini-Hochberg across the 12 cells.

```
 model      measure         p_word  p_word_BH    p_item  p_item_BH
 mgpt_sc    gaze_rt        0.0120*    0.0144*   0.0327*     0.1248
 mgpt_sc    total_rt       0.0010*    0.0045*   0.0290*     0.1248
 mgpt_sc    firstfix_rt    0.0060*    0.0103*   0.0347*     0.1248
 mgpt_lc    gaze_rt        0.0005*    0.0045*   0.0703      0.1250
 mgpt_lc    total_rt       0.0015*    0.0045*   0.0784      0.1250
 mgpt_lc    firstfix_rt    0.0015*    0.0045*   0.0520      0.1248
 monot_30m  gaze_rt        0.0030*    0.0072*   0.0417*     0.1248
 monot_30m  total_rt       0.0070*    0.0105*   0.0937      0.1250
 monot_30m  firstfix_rt    0.0260*    0.0260*   0.1608      0.1755
 monot_all  gaze_rt        0.0090*    0.0120*   0.0888      0.1250
 monot_all  total_rt       0.0060*    0.0103*   0.1140      0.1368
 monot_all  firstfix_rt    0.0220*    0.0240*   0.1774      0.1774

 * = p < .05
 significant after BH: per-word 12/12, item-level 0/12
```

Long-context mGPT (`mgpt_lc`) goes from p ~ 0.001 (per-word) to ~ 0.05-0.08
(item-level, pre-BH), and nothing survives BH at the item level on English alone.
This is meant as a diagnostic companion, not a replacement for the pooled
cross-language analysis.

## Entropy contrasts (English)

`analysis_ent.Rmd` tests two contrasts against the surprisal model. Both are run
here with the same item-level treatment (`item_level_reanalysis_ent.R`), with BH
within each contrast. `dLL` / `dR2` are relative to the surprisal model.

### add: does entropy add over surprisal?  (surp + ent) vs (surp)

```
 model      measure           dLL      dR2   p_word  p_word_BH   p_item  p_item_BH
 mgpt_sc    gaze_rt      -0.00080   0.0001   0.6162     0.6162   0.7879     0.7879
 mgpt_sc    total_rt     -0.00182  -0.0008   0.0415*    0.1244   0.1386     0.2377
 mgpt_sc    firstfix_rt  -0.00083  -0.0004   0.5107     0.5572   0.6209     0.6774
 mgpt_lc    gaze_rt       0.00690   0.0037   0.0230*    0.1244   0.0249*    0.0703
 mgpt_lc    total_rt      0.00921   0.0059   0.0125*    0.1244   0.0227*    0.0703
 mgpt_lc    firstfix_rt   0.00487   0.0032   0.0535     0.1283   0.0293*    0.0703
 monot_30m  gaze_rt       0.00237   0.0015   0.2524     0.4326   0.0857     0.1713
 monot_30m  total_rt      0.00185   0.0015   0.4058     0.4894   0.1901     0.2558
 monot_30m  firstfix_rt   0.00510   0.0036   0.0340*    0.1244   0.0081*    0.0483*
 monot_all  gaze_rt       0.00136   0.0008   0.4078     0.4894   0.1918     0.2558
 monot_all  total_rt      0.00189   0.0013   0.4028     0.4894   0.2902     0.3483
 monot_all  firstfix_rt   0.00317   0.0023   0.1114     0.2229   0.0068*    0.0483*

 * = p < .05 ;  significant after BH: per-word 0/12, item-level 2/12
```

Entropy adds almost nothing over surprisal: `dLL` and `dR2` sit near zero, and
after BH the per-word test finds nothing while the item-level test flags only two
first-fixation cells. Note the item-level test is not uniformly more conservative
here: for a few small but text-consistent effects (the monot first-fixation cells)
it is slightly more powerful than the per-word test, which is the honest behaviour
once independent units are counted correctly.

### replace: entropy in place of surprisal.  (ent) vs (surp)

```
 model      measure           dLL      dR2   p_word  p_word_BH   p_item  p_item_BH
 mgpt_sc    gaze_rt      -0.00461  -0.0021   0.2509     0.4301   0.4367     0.7486
 mgpt_sc    total_rt     -0.01352  -0.0082   0.0080*    0.0960   0.0430*    0.5155
 mgpt_sc    firstfix_rt  -0.00483  -0.0029   0.1249     0.3608   0.2189     0.6795
 mgpt_lc    gaze_rt      -0.00144  -0.0009   0.7866     0.8859   0.8780     0.8955
 mgpt_lc    total_rt     -0.00368  -0.0022   0.5842     0.8762   0.7261     0.8955
 mgpt_lc    firstfix_rt  -0.00114  -0.0008   0.8121     0.8859   0.8543     0.8955
 monot_30m  gaze_rt      -0.00673  -0.0035   0.1629

body:
Closes #188

## What this adds

**`mutants.yml`**: runs each package's `test:mutants` driver.
- **When:** nightly on `next`, `workflow_dispatch`, PRs that edit `packages/*/test-harnesses/**` or this workflow, and PRs labelled `run-mutants`.
- A `select` job decides whether to run, rather than an `on: paths:` filter, so a PR that doesn't qualify gets skipped jobs instead of a missing check run.
- One job per package, each on its own runner. The drivers rewrite source in place, so no other test run shares the working tree.
- A failed nightly run opens an issue titled "Nightly mutation harness run failed", or comments on it if one is already open.
- A run started by an unrelated label gets its own concurrency group, so it cannot cancel a real run.

**`--check-anchors`** on both drivers: asserts every anchor matches exactly once, without mutating or running vitest. `build.yml` runs it before install on every PR, so a stale anchor fails the PR that made it stale instead of reporting `SKIP`. Every rot case in #188 was this kind.

**Root scripts:** `test:mutants` runs both packages one at a time; `test:mutants:anchors` runs the anchor check.

The Server driver now uses `pnpm exec vitest run`, matching ActivitySync.

## Verification
- `pnpm run test:mutants:anchors`: 80 + 16 anchors match.

body:
#### 6730df1f8510e66b8bc744273178c52d72d99199 
[JSC] Prepare visitChildren and marking constraints for a SlotVisitor that marks more than one heap
https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=325294
rdar://188409763

Reviewed by Yusuke Suzuki and Mark Lam.

Each Heap has its own Collector, and each Collector its own SlotVisitors, so today a visitor's VM and
Heap are always those of the cell or constraint it is working on. We want one Collector to mark
several heaps. Its visitors will then have no heap of their own, so code that asks a visitor for "its"
heap has to ask the cell or the constraint instead:

 * FunctionExecutable, JSWeakObjectRef, JSFinalizationRegistry, and the Objective-C and GLib
   JSAPIWrapperObject ask the cell.
 * The output constraint captures its Heap, as the other core constraints already do.
 * JITWorklist::visitWeakReferences takes the VM from its caller.

Asking the cell loads the VM from its block header. FunctionExecutable does so next to an IsoCellSet
update that reads the same header, and JSFinalizationRegistry and the API wrappers next to work that
costs far more. For JSWeakObjectRef the load can miss in cache; A/B testing showed no change.

The remaining uses of SlotVisitor::vm() and SlotVisitor::heap() ask about the collection rather than
a heap, and will be handled separately.

No change in behavior so covered by existing tests

body:
## Scope
Refs #240; advances parent #40's local member privacy/export slice.

Adds an owner-only, versioned JSON download for current structured preview records. Reads the profile and 11 record sections in one repeatable-read transaction; denies missing, expired, revoked or staff sessions; refuses over 100 records or 256 KiB rather than truncating. The UI states that evidence bytes are a separate export and that this is not a full portability response.

## Evidence
- Exact clean local commit and unbypassed pre-push `make verify` passed after rebasing onto #239's merged main. See generated `artifacts/application-verification.json` for SHA/tree and raw counts.
- 57 repository, 417 unit, 75 real PostgreSQL integration, 61/61 local journey IDs across desktop/mobile (122 executions), 60/60 critical. Unit statements/functions/lines 100%, branches 99.65%.
- Browser L61 covers owner download, unrelated member isolation and expiry. PostgreSQL tests cover current/deleted/redacted rows, denial, both limits and repeatable snapshot under concurrent update.
- Provisional full-MVP tranche: 18/18; approved full-MVP remains 0/100.

## Self-review and limits
Reviewed all changed files and diff against #240; no blocking finding. SQL uses fixed table/column lists and a member ID derived only from current token; response carries no token hash. Errors do not expose member text. No schema migration, provider integration or deployment. This is self-review, not independent security/privacy approval. Hosted retention, backup expiry, derivatives, billing, live terms and full release evidence remain on #40/#42/PLAN-002. Rollback is route/UI/wiring removal; no data migration.

author: marcuspat
body:
## Summary

`sentinel serve --mcp` turns Sentinel into a deny-by-default policy gate that any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, …) can call over stdio. The agent can **ask** and **propose**. It cannot **approve** or **execute**: the gate has no code path to approval, and approval and execution are separate operator commands.

New crate: `sentinel-mcp`. It reuses `PolicyEvaluator`/`default_policy`, `AuditLog`, `Plan`/`PlanStep` and the `Capability` trait, and adds no new dependencies.

| Tool | Host effect |
|---|---|
| `sentinel_capabilities` | none |
| `sentinel_policy_check` | none. Dry `PolicyEvaluator::evaluate`; returns allow/deny/require_approval/audit_only + `matched_rule` |
| `sentinel_investigate` | runs one capability, only if its manifest kind is `ReadOnly` (structural check) **and** policy allows it |
| `sentinel_propose_plan` | validates every step (args + policy) and stores a `PendingApproval` plan. **Never executes.** Any denied, unknown or invalid step means nothing is stored. Risk tier comes from the manifest, not from the agent |
| `sentinel_plan_status` | none |

Operator side: `sentinel plans | show-plan | approve | reject | execute`.
- `approve` needs a TTY on stdin plus a typed id prefix, and pins the plan's SHA-256 content hash.
- `execute` refuses anything not `Approved`, or whose content no longer matches the approved hash (even if `content_hash` was recomputed). It re-evaluates policy per step, halts on the first deny or failure, and runs each plan at most once.
- Every `tools/call` is audited as the new `AuditEventType::McpToolCalled` **before** dispatch, followed by the usual policy and capability events. Unknown tools such as `sentinel_approve` are audited too.
- Each process writes its own hash-chained JSONL under `<state-dir>/audit/`, verifiable with `sentinel verify-audit`.

Also changed: tracing now goes to **stderr for all subcommands** (it was stdout), so the JSON-RPC stream stays clean.

Design: `docs/adr/ADR-013-mcp-policy-gate.md`. Roadmap: `plans/SPEC-mcp-gate-and-arena.md`.

## Implemented vs spec-only

**Implemented + tested:** spec part A (MCP gate, plan store, CLI `approve`/`reject`/`execute`/`plans`/`show-plan`), ADR-013, and the README section with a Claude Code `.mcp.json` example plus `permissions.deny` rules. CHANGELOG and CONTRIBUTING are updated.

**Spec only, nothing deployed or published:**
- **Sentinel Arena** (part B): Fly Machines recommended for v1 over E2B, self-hosted Firecracker and containers, with reasons. Also covers abuse controls, a hard cost ceiling with the formula (vendor prices quoted with their fetch date) and plan-before-apply IaC.
- **crates.io naming** (part C). Checked via the crates.io API on 2026-09-25. **`sentinel-core` and `sentinel-tui` are already taken by other projects**, so the opt-in publish job in `release.yml` would fail at its first crate. Recommendation: publish the binary as `sentinelctl` (available) and mark the libraries `publish = false` for now.
- **Milestones M1–M7** with acceptance criteria (part D).
- Workflow changes are proposed in the spec, not made: add `sentinel-mcp` to the release `CRATES` and add a fmt step to CI.

## Test output (run on a fresh clone of this branch)

```
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 9.88s      (exit 0)

cargo test --workspace   (exit 0)
  sentinel_mcp unit (store):   test result: ok. 7 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
  sentinel-mcp/tests/gate.rs:  test result: ok. 13 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
  sentinel-tui/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
  workspace total (sum of all "test result" lines): 434 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored
  (main before this PR: 413 passed; this PR adds 21)
```

What the tests assert:
- `propose_plan` spawns zero commands: the real capabilities run against a counting fake executor.
- An unapproved plan cannot run, and a plan edited after approval cannot run.
- Approval is single-shot.
- `sentinel_approve` doesn't exist (-32602) and is still audited.
- stdout of `serve --mcp` is pure JSON-RPC.
- A piped (non-TTY) `sentinel approve` fails.
- Every chain passes `sentinel verify-audit`.
- Framing: parse errors, batches, notifications and a >1 MiB line.

**`cargo fmt --all --check`: fails. The failure is pre-existing on `main` and not introduced here.** `main` already has fmt diffs in 45 files. Every file this PR adds passes `rustfmt --check`. Existing files edited here (`main.rs`, `events.rs`, `log.rs`) keep main's formatting so the diff stays reviewable. I made a formatting-only commit (`cargo fmt --all`, 45 files) locally, but `git push` was refused by the session's git proxy. Pushing through the GitHub API means sending whole files, and I didn't hand-transcribe 17.8k lines. Suggest a separate `cargo fmt --all` commit, then the CI fmt step from the spec.

## Known gaps / decisions for Marcus

1. **Same-UID shell defeats the TTY check.** I verified this: `script -qec "sentinel approve <id>"` approves. A same-UID process can also edit the state dir. The real boundary is a dedicated user for the gate and state dir; README/ADR document this and recommend Claude Code deny rules as defence in depth.
2. **`RequireApproval` semantics differ.** `sentinel execute` treats operator plan approval as satisfying `RequireApproval`. The existing `ReasoningLoop::execute_plan` skips those steps even after approval, so under the default policy `sentinel run` never executes Medium-risk mutating capabilities (`log_vacuum`, `cache_prune`, `service_start`). This is pre-existing; unifying the executors is spec follow-up A.7.2.
3. No rollback in `sentinel execute`: it halts on the first failure. No TUI approval yet. No store locking (race between concurrent `execute` calls).
4. **`Cargo.lock` is not updated in this branch** (API push limitation). CI doesn't use `--locked`, so it resolves automatically; commit the lock after `cargo build`. It only adds the `sentinel-mcp` entry.
5. Commit `b3385b7` accidentally set `Cargo.toml` to a placeholder; the next commit, `3c889d2`, restores it. Squash-merge recommended.
6. Crate naming decision (spec part C).
